7.19.m:
Vyāsa said:
For those people who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa, endowed with devotion,
misfortune never exists, O best of the twice-born.

Once more I will proclaim the glorification of the Lord of Kamalā,
hearing which all mortals attain the supreme state.

Hearing the glorification of Vāsudeva, Vaiṣṇavas are satisfied;
heretics are not satisfied, partaking of misery in hell.

The supreme glorification of Viṣṇu should never be spoken in the presence of heretics,
O best of the twice-born; it must be spoken before Vaiṣṇavas.

Formerly, in the Tretā age, O twice-born Jaimini, there was a king of the earth
who was constantly addicted to sin and intent upon reviling dharma.

He seized the property of brāhmaṇas, O best of the twice-born, was eager for intercourse with other men's wives,
ate cow flesh, drank liquor, and was greedy for the coquetry of prostitutes.

He was a slayer of those who came for refuge, constantly a defamer of others,
a betrayer of trust, a killer of friends, and likewise an oppressor of his kinsmen.

He spoke falsely, was cruel, kept company with heretical people,
deprived twice-born men of their livelihood, and stole deposits.

Observing that he was such a wicked man, devoted to sin,
all his kinsmen, enraged, came to his house.

The kinsmen said:
“The reputation that was earned by our ancestors in our spotless lineage,
that reputation, O fool, is being led to ruin by you.
"Abandoning the path of dharma, you constantly commit sin; / destroying the fame of my lineage, you were born to bring sorrow to your kinsmen.

The Creator's work of creation in you is regarded as very astonishing:
in the ocean where the moon was born, poison also came into existence!

Ah, the destructive power of bad sons cannot be reckoned!
It instantly destroys the fame accumulated over many generations.

When an excellent son is born, even a lowly lineage becomes noble;
but when a son is lowly, even a noble lineage falls into degradation.”

Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, all those kinsmen, fearing infamy and filled with anger,
instantly abandoned him, the worst of sinners, O twice-born.

Abandoned by his kinsmen and reviled by all people,
deprived of all wealth and miserable, he resorted to banditry.

As he practiced the deeds of a bandit, pitiless and harming others,
all the people of the countryside seized him and reported him to the king.

Because of affection for his father, O best of the twice-born, that wicked man
was not executed by that ruler of the earth, but was expelled from his own country.

Then, taking refuge in a forest along with many arrogant bandits,
that merciless man waited in order to rob travelers of their property.

Once, O Jaimini, exhausted from wandering in the forest,
he went to the bank of a river with the bandits in order to bathe.

At that river, that wicked-minded man saw many people
having the appearance of brāhmaṇas, devoted to the worship of the Blessed Lord.

Then all those brāhmaṇas, having worshipped Janārdana,
conversed with one another out of great joy concerning the deeds they had done:

“Today campaka flowers were offered by me;”
and another said: “Betel was given by me to Murāri.”
"Betel must never be chewed by me, even in any birth; / today an excellent plantain fruit was offered by me to Hari."

"And through birth after birth, plantain fruit must not be eaten by me." / Someone says, "A pomegranate was offered by me to Hari;"

someone says, "An excellent mango was offered by me." / And having heard the words of those [men] speaking thus to one another,
Urvīśu pondered: "What shall I offer to Viṣṇu? / Whatever edible objects there are in the world, those I
cannot abandon; what shall I offer to Murāri? / I am always dwelling in the middle of forests, a thief terrified of the king;
I have indeed no right ever to ride in a cart." / Vyāsa said: Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, that robber again and again
offered a cart to Hari, the bestower of the four aims of life. / Then all those brāhmaṇas, O twice-born, departed as they had come.
That robber also, along with the robbers, went to his own abode. / Once, along that very path, a certain traveler,
carrying a basket of molasses, arrived in the Kākī district. / Then that robber, fearless and injuring others, suddenly
seized that traveler's basket of molasses. / Then those robbers broke open the basket of molasses,
and to Urvīśu's share fell a cart made of molasses. / Urvīśu, having received that cart made of molasses, O best of the twice-born,
pondered in his mind, remembering his words: / "Formerly, a cart was indeed offered by myself to Murāri;
therefore, a cart must not be taken by me ever in this birth." / Thinking thus in his heart, that cart made of molasses was given
to a certain brāhmaṇa to cause pleasure to Mādhava. / Recognizing that devotion of that great sinner, O twice-born,
Janārdana, immediately pleased, took away all his sin. / On that very day, O twice-born, having entered the great forest,
that Urvīśu was slain by all the furious citizens. / Then, to fetch him, the Blessed One [sent] a chariot made of gold,
and sent messengers adorned with various ornaments. / Then those messengers of the Blessed One, [placing] that Urvīśu whose sins were gone
upon the chariot, immediately went to Hari's city. / Then, having attained proximity to Hari, that best of virtuous souls,
after remaining in the presence of Keśava for a hundred manvantaras, / attained supreme knowledge and entered the body of Hari.
Vyāsa said: By whatever means a man practices devotion to Hari, / he goes across to the other shore of the ocean of worldly existence like a royal swan.
In whose mind devotion to Hari exists even for a moment, / he goes to that supreme abode; even a sinful soul goes [there].
Having offered even a single excellent object to Murāri, / it should be enjoyed by oneself alone afterwards for the pacification of sin.
Whatever object has been offered to Hari, that he should give to a twice-born; / the wise must by no means consume any remnant of it themselves.
Whatever objects are sweet, O best of brāhmaṇas, / without offering them to Viṣṇu, they must not be consumed by Vaiṣṇavas.
The glorification of the food offering to Viṣṇu destroys all sins; / along with a legendary history, I shall speak it again: listen attentively, O twice-born.
There was a brāhmaṇa named Sarvajani, born of a pure lineage, / calm, self-controlled, endowed with compassion, a worshiper of gurus and brāhmaṇas,
intent upon the worship of Hari, devoted to remembering Hari, / destroying the distress of those who surrendered to him, speaking the truth, with conquered senses,
bathing in the morning, observing his own code of conduct, free from violence, / dedicated to the Ekādaśī vow, and intent on honoring his kinsmen.
Once, that best of the twice-born saw Keśava in a dream: / dark, with spotless lotus-eyes, a smiling face, clad in yellow garments,
his body radiant with gold earrings, anklets, and a diadem, / his chest illumined by the Kaustubha gem, adorned with a forest garland,
four-armed, the Lord bearing a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, / endowed with all auspicious marks, wearing a golden sacred thread.
Having obtained the vision of the Lord of the world in a dream, that twice-born, / with folded hands and hair bristling with joy on his body, praised Him:

"Praise be to You, the supporter of the entire universe, / the destroyer of grief, fear, and disease for virtuous people, / to Nārāyaṇa, dear to Kamalā's heart, / to You who grant dharma, wealth, pleasure, and the supreme nectar [of liberation]!

All sins indeed were committed by me, / intoxicated and perpetually overcome by delusion, O Murāri; / therefore I am afraid of the deep ocean of worldly existence; / rescue me by granting Your own boat of devotion!
Although a man knows sin, O Hari, / he quickly attains delusion on earth, O enemy of Kaiṭabha; / even so, I continually commit sin with joy; / therefore, no person is as utterly foolish as I am.

The tree of merit suddenly bears the fruit of happiness; / what do I know, O Man-lion, having committed sin? / I have no wealth for the rite of offering flowering trees; / Lord, be gracious, O Blessed One, what can I do?

Having abandoned the pair of Your lotus-feet, the place of supreme nectar, / this bee of my mind, under the delusion that it is a lotus, / goes, O God, to a woman's face which brings death / and is continually sprinkled with phlegm.

My hand is devoid of giving; my mouth speaks untruth; / and both ears are always eager for listening to sin; / destroy these faults of mine, O Hari, of Your servant, / because, O Lord, You are truly the destroyer of the faults of the surrendered.

In the dreadful ocean of worldly existence, O Man-lion, at some time, / a very steady boat of devotion to You was attained by me here; / even there, subject to fate, alas, an evil-minded one, / my time of suffering only persists continually.

Is there a shining path for going to the other shore of worldly existence, / free from all sorrow, compassionate and gracious? / For me, blinded by the great darknesses of delusion, / my vision never falls upon You here, O Viṣṇu.

Even though I am a sinful soul, this mind of mine, O Murāri, is not lost— / [the mind] which destroys the suffering of ruined people— / since, O slayer of Keśin, O Lord, I behold You today even in a dream, / whose lotus-feet are praised by all the gods!"
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by him, the blessed God, the husband of Kamalā, / knowing how to speak, who carries [one] across the ocean of worldly existence, spoke words.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am ever pleased with your devotions, O best of the twice-born; / therefore, very soon indeed, everything will become auspicious for you.
Even though you were a sinner, your deliverance was performed by Me previously, O twice-born; / now you are My devotee, no misfortune will occur."
The brāhmaṇa said: / "Who was I previously, O Viṣṇu, or what sin was committed by me? / How was my deliverance previously performed by You, though I was a sinner?
How was I born in this worldly existence, and how was I brought forth by You? / Tell all this, O Lord, since You are always compassionate."
The Blessed Lord said: "Although this is a secret not to be revealed, O best of the twice-born, / nevertheless, out of affection for you, I shall speak; listen.
Formerly, O best of brāhmaṇas, born in the race of birds, / you came to be in the regions of the earth through the ripening of your own karma."
Constantly agitated by hunger and thirst, / you wandered about eating insects and the hot water of a mountain stream.
Always experiencing various miseries, born in the womb of a bird, / you remained on earth in former times for four thousand years.
Once, a brāhmaṇa named Kulabhadra, who knew all principles, / worshipped me with devotion on a riverbank with food offerings and other rites.
Having worshipped me, that best of brāhmaṇas discarded the uncooked grains of my food offering / right there, and then went back to his home.
Then, coming down from a tree, hungry as a bird, / you ate all the rice grains belonging to my food offering.
Having merely eaten [them], you were immediately freed from extremely terrible sins. / Sometime later, your time having arrived, O brāhmaṇa, you went the way of death.
My own messengers were sent to bring you by all means; / then, placing you—whose sins were destroyed—upon a chariot,
all the hosts of messengers reached the supreme abode at once. / You remained in my presence for thousands of crores of cosmic ages,

enjoying all pleasures difficult to obtain even by the gods. / Then you were born, O best of brāhmaṇas, in a pure lineage of brāhmaṇas.

Even there, your devotion to me has become exceedingly firm again; / having worshipped me continually through practical yoga, O best of the twice-born,"
at the end of your life, by my grace, you will attain my abode. / When I am pleased, O brāhmaṇa, even a sinner partakes of liberation;
if ever I am angry with someone, even a meritorious soul partakes of sin. / Therefore, O brāhmaṇa, welfare unto you! You are my devotee, O one of good vows.
I shall give you the supreme station, which cannot be obtained even by the gods. / The brāhmaṇa said: / By your grace, O Lord, my past account has been heard by me.
Now I wish to hear whatever you will speak of, O Lord. / With whom are you pleased, O Indra of gods, or with whom are you angry, O Lord?
Out of great compassion, you should tell me all of this. / The Blessed Lord said: / By which action, O best of brāhmaṇas, satisfaction arises in my heart,
and by which anger [arises], all that I shall tell in brief. / One who is compassionate, O best of brāhmaṇas, toward all living beings at all times,
and free from egoism—with him I am always pleased. / He who performs action for my sake, endowed with dharma and devotion,
who speaks what is tranquil for my sake—with him I am always pleased. / The human being who, having obtained sweet food, gives it to me,
who is the same in honor and dishonor—with him I am always pleased. / The human being who knows me as dwelling in the bodies of all living beings,
who is free from doing violence to others—with him I am always pleased. / But he who performs actions having deliberated well again and again,
who desires the welfare of cows and brāhmaṇas—with him I am always pleased. / He who diligently keeps a promise made by himself,
who diligently goes to one who has surrendered—with him I am always pleased. / He who gives gifts to those who cannot repay him, O best of brāhmaṇas,
whose mind is always fixed on me—with him I am always pleased. / By which action I am pleased has been stated in brief.
Now listen to those actions by which I am angered, O brāhmaṇa: / He who takes delight in violence to others and is pitiless toward all creatures,
proud and always angry—he brings me to enmity. / He who speaks falsehood, who is cruel, and who is intent upon censuring others,
who destroys the livelihood of a poet—he brings me to enmity. / A fool who, out of delusion, abandons his father and mother who are without visible fault,
as well as his wife, brother, and sister—he brings me to enmity. / That foolish-minded man who scolds his parents,
who disrespects his guru, O brāhmaṇa—he brings me to enmity. / Those who cut down pleasure groves and those who destroy reservoirs of water,
and those who destroy villages—they bring me to enmity. / Those people who look upon another's wife and fall into despondency,
and who listen to sinful conversation—with them I am always angry. / Those fools who hate their master, those who seize the property of the helpless,
and those who betray trust—with them I am always angry. / Those who destroy the semen of a bull, those who are husbands of low-caste women,
and those who cut down an aśvattha tree—with them I am always angry. / Those who make divisions among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna,
and those excessively attached to others' wives—with them I am always angry. / Those sinful-minded men who eat on the eleventh lunar day out of greed,
and those who revile the Vedas—with them I am always angry. / Those who take pleasure in sinful thoughts, and those who delight in betraying friends,
and those who destroy an āmalakī tree—with them I am always angry. / Those who, deluded by desire, engage in sexual intercourse during the daytime,
and also with a menstruating woman—with them I am always angry. / Those who, out of delusion, approach a woman who has not yet seen her menses, O good one,
and always those villains [who approach] a woman observing a vow—they bring me to enmity. / And those who eat food at night on the new moon day,
and two meals on Sunday—with them I am always angry. / Meat, sexual intercourse, and oil on the new moon day, O brāhmaṇas—
with those who do not abandon these, O best of brāhmaṇas, I am always angry. / What is the use of speaking much here? I shall tell you in brief:
Those who revile Vaiṣṇavas—with them I am always angry. / Vyāsa said: / Having spoken thus, Lord Viṣṇu suddenly vanished.
And that brāhmaṇa, having given up sleep, arose from his bed. / By the word spoken by Keśava, that brāhmaṇa who practiced devotion to Hari,
abandoned all work and became devoted to practical yoga. / Even from eating the food offering of Nārāyaṇa this was the fruit;
what might be the result for men who perform worship of Hari, I do not know. / I tell you in brief, listen, O best Jaimini:
Having performed the worship of Hari even once, the supreme abode is attained. / Human birth is hard to obtain in the world, and there worship of the discus-bearer is even harder;
devotion even there, O best of brāhmaṇas, is proclaimed to be rare.

A man in whose mind there is the desire to cross the ocean of saṃsāra filled with all kinds of misery / should, as a noble person, constantly perform the worship of Vāsudeva with devotion amidst all duties.

7.20.m: Vyāsa said: / The fruit of Viṣṇu's worship has been told by me in brief, O brāhmaṇa; / now I shall speak of gifts; listen with concentrated mind.
Between the two, giving gifts and asceticism, the gift alone is considered supreme. / By asceticism sin is consumed, it is said; there is no sin in the act of giving.
Asceticism is best in the Kṛta age, and meditation in the Tretā age; / worship is best in the Dvāpara age, and giving gifts is best in the Kali age.
Therefore, in the Kali yuga, giving gifts for the satisfaction of the Lord of Kamalā / should constantly be performed by wise men desiring the supreme abode.
Just as a digit of the moon grows digit by digit, / such is the course proclaimed by wise men for giving gifts and for asceticism.
Accumulation of wealth should be made even by small units, O best of brāhmaṇas; / but the wise person should apply that accumulated wealth to the act of giving.
Even when possessing wealth, that mortal who neither eats nor gives / is to be known as poor, deprived of giving and enjoyment.

With whom does wealth go, and who goes with it, O brahmin?
What was given in the past arrives here when one has met one's death.

Those men who become impoverished by constantly giving gifts—
they are not to be regarded as poor; in the next world they are mighty lords.

Those who guard their wealth out of miserliness are to be known as miserable indeed;
in the end, leaving it all behind, they depart despondent, O Jaimini.

In the other world, O best of brahmins, for one devoid of virtuous power,
destitute of wealth and bereft of kin, what was not given does not wait upon him.

Even little by little, O chief of brahmins, endowed with devotion and faith,
gifts must constantly be given by Vaiṣṇavas according to their own devotion.

Of all gifts, O best of brahmins, the gift of food
and the gift of water are proclaimed by knowers of the truth to be the very highest.

Without food, the vital breaths do not remain in the bodies of the embodied;
the giver of food is known as the giver of life, and the giver of life gives everything.

Therefore, the giver of food obtains the fruit of all gifts;
and the gift of water is equal to the gift of food, O Jaimini.

Without water there can be no food; therefore water is given.
Hunger and thirst, O chief of brahmins, are proclaimed to be equal.

Therefore, the giving of water also is spoken of as supreme by the wise.
Water is the life of men; without water there is no life.

Therefore, for the sake of preserving life, the wise person should give water.
By whomsoever food and water are given on the surface of the earth, O chief of brahmins,

by him all gifts have been performed—there is no doubt of this.
Listen to the glorification of the gift of food and of the gift of water.

In Hāstinapura there was a wealthy man, rich like Kubera;
in that very city there was a courtesan, beautiful as a divine maiden,

known as Ratividagdhā, endowed with all auspicious marks.
There, a brahmin woman named Kṣemaṅkarī, born of an excellent lineage,

endowed with all good qualities, a twice-born man's daughter, had become a widow.
That brahmin woman, O best of brahmins, her mind attached to a paramour,

performing forbidden acts and having abandoned her senses, fell into folly.
In her company, O brahmin, both the courtesan and that brahmin woman,

taking up the conduct of a courtesan, formed a friendship in affection.
That courtesan and the brahmin woman, both together day by day,

fondly committed countless sins, O Jaimini.
Then that Ratividagdhā reached old age,

as did the brahmin woman, O chief of brahmins, ill-behaved and exceedingly sinful.
Once, that foremost of courtesans, grown old, to that friend of hers

spoke, full of humility, astonished, O brahmin.
Ratividagdhā said:
“Friend, together with you I have committed many terrible sins.

Even today, my great inclination toward sin remains;
yet my beauty and my strength have all been taken away by old age.

Thus producing constant infirmity, craving cannot be abandoned.
Great immobility has been attained by me, a sinner.

Death seems as if arrived now, when seen as imminent.
The riches that were indeed acquired by me through sin—

who will preserve them when I, childless, am dead?
Therefore, all these riches, even those unjustly gained,

I wish to give to brahmins, if you agree, my friend.”
The brahmin woman said: “Whatever riches were gathered by me, see,

all of them were continually given to unworthy recipients;
therefore, deprived of wealth, what shall I give to a twice-born?

If you have wealth, quickly make a gift of it then.”
Having heard her words, that courtesan was exceedingly delighted.

With all her wealth she performed the gift of food.
And there was a wealthy brahmin, O chief of brahmins, named Hariśarman, who with great devotion

constantly worshipped the Blessed One, Janārdana;
with subdued senses, anger conquered, free from violence and deceit,

he performed great austerity for the pleasure of Kamalā's lord.
With fragrant perfumes, flowers, offerings of food, clarified butter, incense, and lamps,

he constantly worshipped Janārdana, the lord of gods.
Yet, though wealthy, this brahmin was fearful of the loss of his wealth.

Ants, mice, and other creatures as well,
in the house of that miser, O best of brahmins, were constantly hungry.

All the wealth he acquired, he enjoyed entirely by himself day by day,
O best of brahmins, avoiding the act of giving.

With his friends, brahmins, and kinsmen he never
even conversed, for fear of a request for money.

Counting up his very plentiful treasures in his own abode,
and thinking himself superior, he rejoiced, O best of brahmins.

In time, that exceedingly wealthy brahmin met his appointed hour;
and that courtesan and that brahmin woman died at the same time, O brahmin.

Then exceedingly terrible messengers came to fetch them,
messengers of the divine Dharmarāja, with nooses and clubs in their hands.

Those messengers, Caṇḍa and the others, taking them, O Jaimini,
went straightway to the city of Dharma by an impassable path.

Caṇḍa said:
“Hariśarman has been brought, and the courtesan, and that brahmin woman.
By your command, O lord of the living, behold them standing before you.”

Beholding them, the lord of the living laughed, O best of twice-born,
and spoke to Citragupta, who is skilled in every matter.

Yama said:
“Examine all their deeds from the very beginning, both auspicious and inauspicious,
O wise, highly intelligent Citragupta!”

Then, by Yama's order, the discerning Citragupta
examined everything, the auspicious deeds and likewise the inauspicious.

Citragupta said:
“Listen, O lord, I will declare the merit as well as the sin
that this courtesan, the brahmin woman, and Hariśarman have committed.

This courtesan named Ratividagdhā, of extremely wicked intention—
the sins that she committed cannot even be recounted.

Yet with all her wealth acquired by unjust means, O son of the Sun,
this courtesan, whose youth had passed, made gifts of food.

Through the power of the gift of food, which grants release from the abode of torment,
she was freed from all sins, even those accumulated over ten million births.

Those people on earth who perform the gift of food, O great king,
even if sinful, go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

As many food-gifts as men bestow on the circle of the earth,
so many killings of brahmins are destroyed for them; of this there is no doubt.

Leaving the bodies of those who give food, sin
suddenly enters into the recipients who accept it, O son of the Sun.

Therefore, the discerning do not accept the food of sinners;
those fools who accept it out of delusion, they alone partake of the sin.

The auspicious and inauspicious deeds of the courtesan have been declared, O lord.
Now hear the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of the brahmin woman.

This brahmin woman named Kṣemaṅkarī, born of a pure lineage,
fond of good renown, committed every kind of sin, O lord.

Abandoning the conduct proper to her stage of life, proud of her own youth,
she became exceedingly sinful, covetous of union with paramours.

Once in her childhood, O king, playing with children,
she dug a four-cornered pit in the street.

On that very day a cloud showered down water,
and that pit dug by her was filled with water, O lord.

Then at midday, a thirsty bull, O king,
tormented by the heat of the sun, drank the water there.
By that alone all her great sins were indeed destroyed, / O wise son of Sūrya, through the power of giving water.
Released from all sins, she may go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa. / For although this evil-minded brāhmaṇa woman committed sins, O Lord of gods,
she is freed from all sins by the power of the gift of water. / And this vipra is a great devotee of the disc-bearing God of gods.
Therefore, over him, Acyuta alone is remembered as the master of living beings.' / Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of Citragupta, the staff-bearing lord [Yama]
saluted that prostitute, that brāhmaṇa woman, and that brāhmaṇa / with heavenly gold ornaments and manifold garments.
Having heard of the worship of them and their families, O Jaimini, / Yama, greatly pleased, spoke these gentle words, smiling:
Yama said: 'You are all noble-souled, with all sins destroyed; / go to the abode of the Lord, the husband of Śrī, which grants all happiness.'
Then Yama, having mounted them upon a heavenly, golden [car] / joined by royal swans, sent them to the abode of the disc-bearer.
Then, mounted on the divine chariot and adorned with all ornaments, / they all, freed from sins, went to the city of the Lord.
Both the courtesan and the brāhmaṇa woman, with all sins destroyed, / attained the presence of the god and dwelt in happiness for a long time, O vipra.
Seeing Hariśarman arriving, Janārdana / affectionately gave him an excellent seat made of gold.
And having worshipped that best of the twice-born with water for the feet, arghya, and sipping water, / Hari, with joy, asked him as he sat on the excellent seat:
The Holy One said: 'O twice-born one, speak of your welfare, for you are the foremost of my devotees. / Dwell long in my temple, free from all afflictions.'
The brāhmaṇa said: 'Remembered or seen, O Lord, one attains welfare, O God; / your presence has been attained by me—what welfare is greater than this?'
Vyāsa said: Hearing his words spoken with affection, / the Lord, being pleased, bestowed his own likeness upon that twice-born one.
The husband of Kamalā gave him all happiness that is hard to attain; / but the Lord gave him no food at all, remembering his miserliness.
After two days had passed, the vipra, foodless and afflicted with hunger, / bowed down in humility and spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of gods.
The brāhmaṇa said: 'O Lord, your abode was attained by the fruits of many austerities; / yet even here, constantly hungry, why am I fruitless, O Lord?
I am fanned upon couches with breezes of white fly-whisks / by groups of celestial maidens endowed with fresh youth.
I am adorned with great garlands of fragrant blossoms, / with all my limbs anointed with sandal, like a foremost king, O Lord.
Lovely-limbed women desiring love constantly dance before me / with singing, by your command, O Nārāyaṇa.
All the gods, beginning with Vāsava, constantly carry on the splendor / of the crowns on their heads the dust of my feet.
Gods, divine sages, and munis, O Lord of the world, / constantly praise me with hymns like servants at all times.
I have four arms, dark [complexion], bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, / eyes like a blossoming lotus, yellow garments, and fine earrings;

wearing a golden sacred thread, crowned, and with earrings, / I am seen by the gods and others just like you, as a second Garuḍa-bannered [Lord].

These hard-to-attain pleasures have been given by you, O Lord; / why do you not give me food, O Supreme Lord?
My body is burning greatly with the fire of hunger, / just like a tree ablaze with a fire located inside its hollow.
This happiness given by you does not please me, O Hari, / when the belly-fire is blazing and my limbs are agitated, O Keśava.
In action, mind, and speech, except for you, the Lord of the world, / no one worshipped by the hosts of gods was worshipped by me.
Even in a dream, O Lord of the universe, devotion was not paid to him. / For what fault, O Lord, do you not give me food?'
Vyāsa said: Then the Lord Viṣṇu, fond of jest, spoke to him: / 'Go quickly to Brahmā, O brāhmaṇa, may good betide you.'
Having heard this speech, the twice-born went quickly to Brahmā; / Brahmā spoke to him, pointing out his wretchedness:
Brahmā said: 'What is earned with hardship and not given to an earthly god, / nor eaten by oneself, that is surely lost—there is no doubt.
The entire cause of your distress has thus been told by me. / Go, O brāhmaṇa, may good betide you; your doubt has been removed.'
The brāhmaṇa said: 'By your favor the fruition of all my own deeds has been heard. / Now tell me, what gifts are to be given by human beings?'
Brahmā said: 'Gifts are manifold; they cannot all be spoken of. / It is told in brief, O vipra; listen attentively.
The gift of land, O best of the twice-born, is the best of the best among all gifts; / he by whose virtuous self it is made should be known as a giver of all gifts.
He who gives land even the size of a cow's hide, O best of the twice-born, / freed from all sins, would go to the supreme abode.
He who gives land with crops to a poor twice-born person— / hear the merit of that man, O best of brāhmaṇas!
Freed from all sins, he would go to the city of Nārāyaṇa; / there he enjoys all happiness as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Having attained the earth again, he would become a universal monarch; / having enjoyed the entire earth for a long time, the man would become Nārāyaṇa.
Because land is to be accepted by the twice-born, even setting aside hundreds of gifts; / both the giver of land and the recipient of land go to heaven.
The foolish twice-born one, however, who rejects the gift of land, / would become exceedingly miserable in birth after birth, O lord among vipras.
He who performs the gift of land even after acquiring it from others— / Viṣṇu, greatly pleased with him, gives the supreme abode.
He who gives a village, O vipra, to a poor twice-born person, / or causes one to be given—hear also his merit:
As many grains of dust as there are on the earth, and as many drops of rain, / for that many manvantaras the wise one would dwell in the realm of Viṣṇu.
He who gives a milch cow along with her calf, O twice-born one— / I will speak of the merit of that noble soul; listen!
The fruit a mortal would obtain by giving the seven-islanded earth filled with crops, / that very fruit he obtains by giving a milch cow to a twice-born person.
He who gives a bull to a brāhmaṇa householder, / freed from dreadful sins, goes to the realm of Rudra.
As many hairs as there are on the body of that bull, / for that many thousands of kalpas he rejoices with Rudra.
He who gives a cow facing both ways to a knower of the Veda— / there is never any return for him from the realm of Rudra.
He who gives a black bull accompanied by sesame seeds / would stay in the mansion of Rudra for the number of those sesame seeds, O best of the twice-born.
And he who gives even a sesame seed's measure of gold to a twice-born person / goes to the abode of Viṣṇu together with ten million members of his family.

One who with devotion gives silver to a destitute twice-born
reaches the realm of the moon and drinks nectar.

And one who gives diamond, pearl, coral, or precious gems,
O best of the twice-born, goes to Śakra's realm.

The noble-minded one who gives a horse, O best of the twice-born,
attains the kingship of the lords of the Gandharvas; of this there is no doubt.

One who gives an elephant that is young and free of defects
becomes a sharer in the kingdom of the gods, like Indra himself, O twice-born.

And one who gives a litter carried by men to a brāhmaṇa, along with a sacrificial fee,
he too attains Indra's station and resides there for four kalpas.

Whoever gives the gift of a Śālagrāma stone to a twice-born,
his merit I shall declare in brief; hear it, O twice-born.

Whatever fruit one obtains by giving the earth with its seven continents, along with mountains, forests, and woods,
that very fruit the giver of a Śālagrāma stone receives.

Whatever fruit is attained by men through the gift of the person weighed against gold,
one giving a Śālagrāma stone receives ten million times more than that.

The one by whom a Śālagrāma stone is given, O best of the twice-born,
by him indeed the fourteen worlds have been given.

The best among men who makes the gift of the person weighed against gold,
clothed in heavenly garments in heaven, becomes a ruler of the earth for a long time.

No rebirth in a mother's womb is found for him again.
Moreover, the best among men who gives a maiden adorned with ornaments

goes to Viṣṇu's abode, free from return [to rebirth].
The foolish man who, out of delusion, sells a maiden

goes to the dreadful hell called Purīṣahrada ('Pool of Excrement').
And the son who is born of a sold maiden, O twice-born,

is to be known as just a cāṇḍāla, cast out from all duties.
A knower of the scriptures should not look upon the face of a man who sells a maiden.

If he should look, even through ignorance, he should look upon the sun.
Whatever religious rite is performed in the presence of a seller of a maiden,

all that auspicious rite comes to naught, O twice-born.
For a seller of a maiden, there is no release again from hell;

for one who gives a maiden, there is no return again from heaven.
What is the use of speaking much here? I tell you in brief:

the fruit of [giving] diamonds, land, and maidens is a hundredfold greater.
And one who gives shoes and an umbrella on the earth,

hear his merit indeed; I tell you in brief:
he will live for a hundred years in this world, endowed with all prosperity,

and upon death, having reached Śakra's city, [he resides there] for four hundred kalpas.
One who gives new clothing attains the highest state.

One who gives old clothing, a cow made of silver,
or a menstruating maiden, always goes to hell.

The man who gives fruit, O brāhmaṇa, goes to the abode of the thirty [gods];
there he enjoys fruit like nectar for thousands of kalpas.

The giver of vegetables goes, O brāhmaṇa, to the station of the blessed Śambhu;
there for two kalpas he consumes milk-rice pudding that is difficult for the gods to obtain.

The giver of milk, the giver of curd, the giver of clarified butter, and likewise the giver of buttermilk
indeed attains the drinking of nectar before the blessed Lord Hari.

The man who gives flowers, O brāhmaṇa, and the giver of perfumes, goes to the abode of the gods;
adorned with flowers and perfume, he remains there for thousands of yugas.

The one who makes the gift of a bed, O best of the twice-born, O highest of the twice-born,
having gone to the realm of Brahmā, sleeps on a couch for a long time.

The giver of a lamp and the giver of a seat, freed from all sin,
seated upon a divine lion-throne, is surrounded by rows of burning lamps.

The man who gives betel, O king, enjoys all auspicious things on earth;
asleep on the lap of a divine woman in heaven, he eats betel indeed.

The best of men who makes the gift of knowledge, O best of the twice-born,
having attained the presence of Viṣṇu, remains there for two hundred yugas.

Then, having attained spiritual knowledge right there, O best of the twice-born,
he attains difficult-to-obtain liberation through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā.

He who teaches a destitute, deeply distressed brāhmaṇa
goes to Viṣṇu's abode, from which return is hard to obtain.

Even a well-born, excellent twice-born does not shine without learning;
therefore, those who teach a twice-born go to the supreme state.

Though he is a visible deity on earth, a brāhmaṇa is a refuge of deities;
yet devoid of learning, the guru of all castes does not shine at all.

Whatever gifts there are in this world, such as gold and the like,
all of them have been given by him by whom a brāhmaṇa has been taught.

The man who, endowed with devotion, makes the gift of a book,
his merit, O best of the twice-born, I declare to you in brief.

As many letters as there are on each and every page in that book,
for each letter he obtains the merit born of giving ten million tawny cows.

As many days as the twice-born recite that book,
for that many manvantaras the giver of the book will reside in Vaikuṇṭha.

Such and many other gifts exist, O earthly deity;
who in this world is capable of describing them fully, even with two hundred [mouths]?

Whatever sins like the killing of a brāhmaṇa are committed by mortals,
those sins are destroyed; therefore one should practice giving.

The gift that is given by the three [upper] castes through their own merit,
as much as the wealth [offered], that much fruit is obtained from that gift.

The gift that is given by people for the pleasure of Kamalā's husband,
from that he obtains ten-million-fold merit; of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, for the sake of Nārāyaṇa's pleasure, a wise person,
endowed with devotional acts, should practice giving, O brāhmaṇa.

Giving is declared by the seers of reality to be superior even to asceticism;
therefore, even with effort, the wise man should perform the act of giving.

The best among men who performs both giving and asceticism—
his equal does not exist in this world, O earthly deity.

7.21.m:
Vyāsa said:
Having heard Brahmā's speech, the excellent twice-born Hariśarman,
bowing down to him once again with devotion, said, O Jaimini:

A brāhmaṇa is the refuge of all deities, a visible god upon earth;
he ferries the giver across the difficult-to-cross ocean of worldly existence.

The glorification of the earthly deities is being declared by me in particular;
out of affection for you, O best of the twice-born, listen with concentrated mind.

The twice-born are the teachers of kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
brāhmaṇas are teachers of one another, and the earthly deities are worthy of worship.

The best of men who worships a brāhmaṇa, regarding him as Viṣṇu,
his lifespan, sons, fame, and prosperity increase.

Whatever fool among men on earth seeks to harm a twice-born,
Keśava desires to sever his head with the Sudarśana discus.

One with flowers in his hand, milk in his hand, or holding a deity's [image], O Jaimini,
or a brāhmaṇa whose body is smeared with oil—a wise person should not bow to him.

One standing in water, standing in a temple, his mind absorbed in meditation,
or performing deity-worship—a wise person should not bow to such a brāhmaṇa.

One answering a call of nature, or eating, O best of the twice-born,
and similarly one chanting the Sāman hymns—a wise person should not bow to such a brāhmaṇa.

Where many brāhmaṇas are gathered together, O best of the twice-born,
a wise person should not offer salutations to each one individually.

He who does not return a greeting with devotion to a twice-born who has greeted him,
should be known as equal to an outcaste, and should never be saluted.

Parents should not bow to their son who has made a bow,
[yet] all twice-born who have made a bow are to be greeted by twice-born.

Wise men do not hate twice-born persons or cows, even if they have committed offenses;
or if they hate them out of delusion, Hari is always angry with them.

He who looks upon begging brāhmaṇas with an angry glance,
Yama pierces needles into his two eyes.

With whichever mouth fools revile a twice-born,
into that very mouth Yama places a glowing iron rod.

In whichever house a brāhmaṇa eats, in that house Keśava himself [eats],
as well as all the deities, ancestors, and celestial sages.

Whatever wise person carries even a single drop of water from the foot of a twice-born,
every sin residing in his body is immediately destroyed.

Whatever sacred pilgrimage places exist across the millions of cosmic universes,
all those sacred places reside in the right foot of a twice-born.

He whose head is constantly sprinkled with water from the foot of a twice-born
has bathed in all sacred places and is consecrated in all sacrifices.

All terrible sins, such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa,
are instantly destroyed for him by bearing water from the foot of a twice-born.

All diseases such as consumption, which cause extreme suffering,
immediately vanish by bearing water from the foot of a twice-born.

Whatever waters are offered at the feet of a twice-born for the sake of the ancestors—
by those the ancestors are satisfied and remain in heaven as long as the moon and stars endure.

Whatever wise person washes the feet of a twice-born and worships them with dūrvā grass,
by him Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, foremost among all gods, is worshipped.

Whatever mortal carries on his head the remnants from the feet of twice-born,
truthfully, truthfully I declare, his liberation is eternal.

That best of men who circumambulates a twice-born and pays homage to him—
by him the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated.

He who offers fruit and betel leaf upon washing the feet of twice-born,
a sick person is freed from illness, and a sinner is freed from sin.

A prisoner is released from bondage upon the washing of the feet of twice-born;
and women who are childless, or women whose children have died,

become mothers of many living children through the washing of the foot of a twice-born.
Hear, O chief of twice-born, the glorification that destroys all sins.

I will tell you briefly of the washing of the feet of the twice-born:
Formerly, there was a man named Bhadrakriya, born in a pure family.

He was a brāhmaṇa devoted to the service of Viṣṇu,
knowing the Vedas, compassionate, serene, and dedicated to devotion to his ancestors.

He offered worship to guests and honored his kinsmen.
Once, that best of twice-born, his body anointed with oil,

went to a pool to bathe, taking his bathing cloth.
Having bathed, that foremost twice-born, in accordance with the rules, performed the water libations and the rest.

Knowing all the scriptures, delighted in the welfare of all people,
having finished his bathing rituals while chanting the names of Hari,

he came to his own house and devoted himself to the worship of Hari.
He washed his two feet with very cool water.

Having washed his feet and hands, that brāhmaṇa, a worshipper of brāhmaṇas,
put away all his bathing accessories.

At the entrance, O best of the twice-born, scorched by the summer sun’s heat
which was like fire, a certain dog arrived.

He fell asleep in that extremely cool water from the brāhmaṇa’s feet.
From the touch of the water from the brāhmaṇa’s feet, the dog, though deeply sinful,

was freed from all sins, even those accumulated over millions of births.
As that dog lay sleeping at the door of the house, distressed by thirst,

he begged for water, but was beaten by the twice-born's servants;
and right there, the dog instantly met his death, O twice-born.

From the touch of the washing of the twice-born’s feet, the dog became free of impurities.
Beholding that great soul who seemed like the Lord in bodily form,

bowed down with humility, that brāhmaṇa, rich in austerities, said:
The brāhmaṇa said: “Tell me, O fortunate one, by what deed, being miserable,
were you born in the breed of dogs, filled with diverse sorrows?”

The [former] dog said: Having heard the words of that twice-born sage, the illustrious one
recounted his entire story from the beginning:

“I was a universal sovereign named Śaṅkha, possessed of great strength.
For four thousand years I ruled over the entire earth.

All sacrifices were performed by me, and my enemies were conquered in battle;
all kinds of gifts were given, and my own kinsmen were protected.

Once, O fortunate one, struck by the arrows of the god of love,
I abducted by force a certain man’s wife who was exceedingly beautiful.

By the power of that sin, my royal fortune fell into jeopardy;
then, though of great strength, I was driven out by all the people.

Deprived of my kingdom, I stayed inside the deep forest.
Exhausted by hunger and thirst, at length I died.

Going to the city of the god of death, I endured misery for a long time.
That is painful to hear, O chief of twice-born, bringing sorrow to the minds of listeners.

On ground made of molten copper, on red-hot iron weapons,
I wallowed amidst intensely terrifying, blazing tongues of fire.

Then, by the command of Yama, a terrifying pillar of iron,
heated red-hot by flaming fire, I was made to embrace and stand.

I was sprinkled by Yama’s servants with streams of cold razor-sharp water,
and other very great suffering was endured by me there in Yama's abode.

Then, with the remainder of my hellish punishment, taking birth again and again
in sinful wombs, great misery was experienced by me for a long time.

By contact with the water of your feet, I am released from the rope of sin;
I am going to the supreme abode, difficult to attain even for yogins.

You are my guru, O best of the twice-born; obeisance to you, great soul!
By your grace I am freed from sins and go to the city of Hari.”

Bhadrakriya said: “O king, a man should never [forget] the story of his previous birth;
therefore, renouncing that, one should always practice righteous conduct.

Whatever king adheres to righteous policy, there is indeed no adversity for him;
he enjoys the earth free of thorns for a long time.

Whatever wicked king takes no pleasure in righteous policy,
he will soon lose his royal fortune; of this there is no doubt.

By a king desiring long life, strength, fame, allies, victory, and happiness,
wise ministers must always be appointed.”
When disregarded by an earthly ruler, the wise respectfully abandon [him]; / in an assembly devoid of the wise, policy is never effective.
Therefore, when policy is ruined, the royal glories of an earthly ruler— / along with treasury, army, and mounts—speedily perish.
Kings who desire their own welfare never hate / brāhmaṇas, astrologers, physicians, or kinsmen.
One who hates astrologers loses his fortune; one who hates physicians is stripped of life; / one who hates kinsmen is left without a family; one who hates the twice-born suffers all afflictions.
Kings are declared to be fathers, and the subjects [their] children; / therefore, earthly rulers should protect their subjects like their own legitimate sons.
One should show such affection toward the city's people as toward one's own son. / Earthly rulers who oppress their subjects are exceedingly sinful;
calamity hovering over their heads is perceived by far-sighted men. / Just as judicious earthly rulers protect their subjects,
so too Hari, the lord of the gods, constantly protects them. / Protection and punishment of the subjects: both bring welfare to a king.
Kings devoid of both should be known as the lowest of kings. / Punishing the wicked and protecting the virtuous—
earthly rulers performing these rejoice long on earth. / An earthly ruler should carefully guard wealth acquired by righteousness.
A vicious earthly ruler, however, would never expand in times of calamity. / Kings desiring their welfare, concerning what is good and bad in their kingdom,
should constantly watch, O best of vipras, expeditiously through the eyes of spies. / As long as danger from a hostile army does not arrive, he should reflect on fear;
but when danger has arrived, the king should act fearless indeed. / Whether toward a kinsman, a friend, a son, or a minister,
he should show gravity on his face, [while holding] affection only in his heart. / Ministers, kinsmen, sons, subjects, and brothers
do not regard an earthly ruler devoid of gravity as a king. / They stand far away at first, and are not [respectful] before him.
People do not desire refuge with an earthly ruler who has abandoned gravity. / A king desiring enduring sovereignty in his entire kingdom
should not employ a single minister for [its] prosperity, O brāhmaṇa; / he would usurp the place of servants of exceedingly sharp intellect.
Therefore, the earthly ruler should employ another servant in the council. / A king who is foolish, ruled by women, constantly devoted to song and instruments,
and devoid of horses and vehicles, speedily goes to ruin. / Observance of right conduct, truth, keeping one's word,

and gravity: these are the marks of earthly rulers, O best of the twice-born. / How is he a king who is devoid of prowess?

How is he a king by whom the hostile land has not been conquered? / Once a hostile land is conquered, for every step the king advances,
at each step he attains the imperishable fruit of a horse sacrifice. / A king desirous of conquering another's territory, slain in battle by kings,
would then go to the supreme abode, freed from all sins. / A king who attains victory in battle reaches the supreme state;
or if he meets death in combat, he obtains the splendor of the king of heaven. / If someone slays a warrior who has cast away weapons, lost his courage,
and is bent on flight, that king goes downward [to hell]. / The one bent on flight in battle and his slayer, O best of the twice-born—
both of them would dwell in an utterly unbearable hell. / But a warrior who fights with courage and his slayer, O best of the twice-born—
both of them would dwell in heaven as long as the moon and sun endure. / What is the use of saying much here? In brief it is said by me:

a king who protects his subjects never comes to ruin.
Brahmā said:
While that earthly ruler whose sins had melted away was speaking thus,
a great shower of flowers fell upon him from the sky, O twice-born. / Then messengers of the noble Keśava arrived,
bringing a beautiful, celestial chariot yoked with royal swans. / Mounting that celestial chariot fashioned of gold,
that king, cleansed of defilement, went to the abode of Viṣṇu. / This glorification of the water from a vipra's feet has been proclaimed to you.
Hearing it with devotional disposition, a man attains liberation. / Thus all that you desired to hear has been told to you;
by what means, O Lord, may my hunger be pacified? / Tell me this, O lord of gods; you are devoted and affectionate to your devotees.

I suffer very great pain, constantly scorched by the fires of hunger.
Brahmā said:
That body which was nourished by you and constantly maintained with meals—
eat the flesh of that body, O best of the twice-born. / Those who gratify themselves with food [taken from] another, / indeed eat the flesh of their own bodies in the next world.

Vyāsa said:
Hearing Brahmā's harsh words, the best of the twice-born / again praised that god with gentle-worded speech.

The brāhmaṇa said:
Be gracious, O god, lord of gods, protector of those who seek refuge! / Forgive all my faults, O best of the gods, homage to you!
In men bearing bodies filled with feces and urine, / faults alone are everywhere, O lord; there are no virtues at all.
The wrongdoing done by me in delusion, you ought to forgive; / a fault in those who have taken refuge is not looked upon by the virtuous.
It is impossible, O Brahmā, to eat the flesh of one's own body; / tell me what is suitable for embodied beings, by which satisfaction may arise.
When this speech had thus been spoken with devotion by that first-born, / the all-knowing Brahmā, fond of brāhmaṇas, spoke compassionately:

Brahmā said:
Do not grieve, O best of vipras; listen to my auspicious word / by which food may be obtained here right now.
A son is born from oneself; as one's self is, so is the son. / Therefore, fathers surely receive [the fruit of] deeds done by a son.
You will stay long in the exceedingly splendid abode of the god. / Having been addressed thus by him, that vipra, afflicted by hunger,

manifested himself in a dream and spoke these words to his son.
The brāhmaṇa said:
You are initiated, O best of sons; may there be the highest auspiciousness for you!
I am your father, gentle one; listen to my distress. / Through the powers of asceticism the supreme abode has been attained by me, O son;
yet, tormented by the fire of hunger, I suffer there continually. / If you now have filial affection for me, O son,
then let food and water be given for my sake, O twice-born. / Whatever is given on the earth's circle by sons for the sake of a father,
the fathers receive that, because sons are born from the father's body. / Formerly, with supreme devotion, the Lord was worshipped by me
with songs, musical instruments, dances, and splendid recitations of praise, / with perfumes, incenses, food offerings, and lamps filled with ghee,
with water for the feet, guest-offerings, sipping-water, meditations, invocations, and the like; / yet by me, a miser, nothing was given to the Lord of the world, my child—
not even food here anywhere as an offering to the Remover of sins. / No worship of a guest with waters or other things was ever performed,
nor was satisfaction given by me to kinsmen and beggars. / By that very karma, O son, even in Nārāyaṇa's abode,
Tormented by the fire of hunger, I suffer every day; / therefore, having quickly given gifts of food and water to a poor twice-born [man],
o best of gods, protect [my] life! / Or, if you do not do so out of cruelty,
then I will surely eat my own flesh right in Viṣṇu's temple!' / Then that hungry brāhmaṇa, with throat, lips, and palate dried up,
Having spoken thus to his initiated son, he suddenly vanished; / then, when the clear morning broke and the sun appeared,
the initiated [son] contemplated what had been spoken by his father in the dream: / 'Due to the fault of his own action, even in the next world my father,
his whole body burned by hunger, suffers every day. / Fie upon me, dull-witted and foremost among wretched people!
Not even a little is given by me for my father's merit.' / Having reflected thus in many ways, the initiated [son], o best of the twice-born,
gave gifts to brāhmaṇas, endowed with faith and devotion. / By the power of that merit, freed from thirst and hunger,
he remained in Nārāyaṇa's abode for as much time as—listen to that! / Four thousand yugas are proclaimed to be a day of Brahmā;
in that very day fourteen Manus occur, / and fourteen Indras are declared on that same day.
They enjoy their respective realms separately, o best of brāhmaṇas. / Having enjoyed their auspicious realms during one day of Brahmā,
fourteen Indras and Manus perish. / While he, Hariśarman, remained in Viṣṇu's world, supremely radiant,
bestowing all happiness, delightful, Brahmā's day passed. / Having enjoyed delightful pleasures there for that much time,
and having attained supreme knowledge, he entered Hari's body. / Vyāsa said: There is no gift in the world equal to food and water, o Jaimini;
the fruits of all gifts indeed [come] from giving food and water. / There is neither examination of the recipient nor restriction of time anywhere
stated by seers of truth regarding gifts of food and water. / Gifts of food and water must always be made.

Men who read with supreme reverence this glorification of food and water and of the twice-born, / having attained the fruit of giving food and water, go in the end to Nārāyaṇa's bliss-bestowing abode.

Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the Kriyāyogasāra Section, [ends] the glorification of giving food and water,

7.22.m: Jaimini said: The auspicious glorification of the Gaṅgā, the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu, / the glorification of giving food, and the excellent [glorification] of giving water,
and the sin-destroying glorification of water that has washed the feet of a brāhmaṇa— / all this, along with legendary history, has been heard by me by your grace, o guru.
Now, o tiger among sages, I desire to hear with reverence / all the fruit of the Ekādaśī, which destroys all sins.
Why is Ekādaśī the best? What rule for it is remembered? / When is it observed, or what is its fruit? Tell me [all] that!
Or what deity is most to be worshipped there, o ocean of good qualities? / What fault would there be for one who does not observe it? You ought to tell me that here.
Vyāsa said: Aside from Nārāyaṇa, no other / is able to declare the entire fruit of Ekādaśī, o brāhmaṇa-seer; therefore, I speak in brief.
Having created the universe with its moving and unmoving beings in the beginning, the supreme Puruṣa, / in order to subdue all beings, created the Person of Sin:
having the slaying of a twice-born as head, the drinking of liquor as eyes, / theft of gold as mouth, and going to the guru's bed as ears;
having the slaying of a woman as nose, the guilt of cow-slaughter as arms, / stealing a deposit as neck, and killing an embryo as throat;
having adultery with another's wife as heart, killing friends as belly, / and slaying those who have sought refuge, etc., from the navel cavity down to the waist;
having abuse of the guru as thighs, selling a maiden as penis, / speaking treacherous words as anus, and killing out of affection as feet;
having minor sins as body hair—a terrifying figure of huge body, / black in color, yellow-eyed, inflicting extreme suffering on those who harbor him.
Seeing that extremely fierce Person of Sin, Puruṣottama, / the Lord, compassionate, who removes the distress of creatures, reflected:
'This wicked and cruel one, bestowing misery on his host, has been created; / in order to subdue creatures, I will create the means for this.'
Then the blessed Viṣṇu himself became the bringer of death, / and he created Raurava and other hells that inflict suffering on sinners.
The fool who indulges in sin does not reach the supreme abode; / by Yama's command he goes there, to the hells such as Raurava.
Once, the blessed Viṣṇu, the destroyer of creatures' distress, / mounting Garuḍa, went to the abode of Yama.
Seeing that Lord of the worlds, Nārāyaṇa, free from affliction, / the son of the Sun, with a delighted mind, worshipped him with incenses and other offerings.
Worshipped by Yama, Viṣṇu, the sole leader of all worlds, / sat on a golden throne, o tiger among the twice-born.
Seated there together with Yama, the blessed slayer of the daityas / heard weeping and lamentation in the southern direction, o lord.
Then the Beloved of Kamalā, his mind filled with wonder, / said to Yama: 'Whence is this sound of weeping among them?'
Yama said: 'O god, the sinners among mortals suffer in hell, which causes extreme misery; / because of the fault earned by their own hands, they languish in my abode.
O Viṣṇu, sinners weep to experience the fruit of the tree of sin, which brings extreme misery; / therefore, that loud sound belongs to them.'
Addressed thus by the son of Sūrya, lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa / went quickly there, where those sinners were weeping.
Seeing those sinful mortals situated in Raurava and other hells, / the Lord, compassion having arisen in his heart, thought:
'All the creatures created by me, due to the fault of their own actions, / languish in hell which causes absolute suffering, even while I am present!'
Having reflected on this and other things, o chief of brāhmaṇas, the compassionate [Lord] / suddenly became the Ekādaśī lunar day right there in person.
Then he caused all those sinners to hear it; / and all of them, their impurities fallen away, went to the supreme abode.
Therefore, know Ekādaśī to be the form of the supreme self, Viṣṇu, / the highest [remedy] for all bad deeds, the best vow among vows.
When the Ekādaśī lunar day had been made, purifying the three worlds, / the Person of Sin, terrified, approached to praise Viṣṇu.
Then, having folded his hands in devotion, that Person of Sin, o twice-born, / praised the beloved of Kamalā, the blessed Janārdana.
Hearing his hymn of praise, the supreme Lord, pleased, / said: 'I am pleased. Say what is desired by you.'
The Person of Sin said: 'O blessed Viṣṇu, I was created to give suffering by your grace; / through the power of Ekādaśī, I am now coming to destruction.
When I am dead in this world, all those embodied beings / will be completely freed from the bonds of worldly existence.
And when all the foremost embodied beings are liberated, / with whom will you play in this playhouse of worldly existence, o Lord?
If you desire to play in the playhouse of the world, / then protect me, o Keśava, from fear of the Ekādaśī lunar day!'
By thousands of other merits, indeed, it is not possible to destroy me; / only the holy Ekādaśī is able to destroy me. Be bestower of a boon!
Among men, beasts, and insects, and also among other living creatures, / in mountains and trees, and in dry places and in waters,
and in rivers and oceans, in forests and wildernesses, / in heaven, in the mortal world, and in the underworld, among gods, gandharvas, and birds—
through fear of the Ekādaśī lunar day, O Viṣṇu, I have fled repeatedly; / nowhere is there a place of safety, nor is there any place whatsoever.
Within millions of cosmic eggs, O eternal God of gods, / on the Ekādaśī lunar day, no place to stay is found by me.
On Ekādaśī, where shall I live without fear, O Lord? / Tell me that, O Lord of gods; I was created by you without cause.
Vyāsa said: / Having spoken thus to Acyuta, the destroyer of distress, the Sinful Person / fell upon the ground and wept, his eyes shedding tears.
Then, laughing, the Blessed Lord, the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, / spoke to the Sinful Person who was terrified by fear of Ekādaśī.
The Blessed Lord said: / Rise up, Sinful Person; cast away grief, make joy! / On the Ekādaśī lunar day, where your dwelling is, that I tell you:
When Ekādaśī arrives, purifying the three worlds, / you must dwell, O Sinful Person, by resorting to food.
As you dwell having resorted to food, O Sinful Person, / this lunar day of Ekādaśī, my form, will not destroy you.
Then the god also disappeared right there, O brahmin sage; / and the Sinful Person, having attained his purpose, departed as he had come.
Therefore, food should never be eaten by the best of people / who desire their own welfare, when the day of Hari has arrived.

All the sins that exist in worldly existence enter into grain
and dwell there on the day of Ekādaśī by the command of glorious Nārāyaṇa.

For those who commit all sins, there may be expiation from hell;
but those who eat grain even on this day should be known as the foremost of sinners.

Again and again I declare firmly: Listen, listen, O people!
One must not eat, one must not eat, one must never eat!

By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, O best of the twice-born,
Ekādaśī, which grants the fruit of the four aims of life, must be observed by all.

Eighteen twinklings of an eye (nimeṣa) are called a kāṣṭhā by the wise;
and thirty kāṣṭhās are called a kalā by those who perceive all truths.

A kṣaṇa consists of thirty kalās, and a muhūrta of twelve kṣaṇas.
Thirty muhūrtas are proclaimed for people as a day and night.

By fifteen of these, a fortnight is to be known, O best of the twice-born;
and by two fortnights, the bright and the dark, a month is reckoned.

In that month, O best of the twice-born, during both fortnights, bright and dark,
even if one is tainted by mortal sin, if one observes Ekādaśī,

freed from all sins, one will attain the world of Viṣṇu.
A mother is not called a mother; the lunar day of Ekādaśī is indeed the mother.

A mother protects only in this world; the lunar day of Ekādaśī protects everywhere.
He who abandons the Ekādaśī vow and performs another vow

casts away a jewel resting in his own hand and grasps a lump of clay, the fool!
Those by whom the Ekādaśī vow is performed with devotion

have performed all sacrifices and all vows.
And those sinful men who eat on Ekādaśī out of delusion,

whether on the bright or on the dark fortnight, Hari is always angered with them;
he who has transgressed that lunar day has transgressed all dharmas.

Just as Viṣṇu is proclaimed supreme among all deities,
so is the Ekādaśī vow the best among all vows.

Just as the sun is supreme among the Ādityas, and the moon among the asterisms,
so is the Ekādaśī vow declared to be the best among all vows.

Just as the sacred fig tree is supreme among trees, and the Sāma is proclaimed among the Vedas,
so is the Ekādaśī vow declared to be the best among all vows.

Just as Uśanas is the foremost of poets, and the Brāhmaṇa among the social classes,
so is the Ekādaśī vow declared to be the best among all vows.

Vyāsa is the best among the sages, and Nārada among the divine seers;
so is the Ekādaśī vow the best among all vows.

Just as the gift of food is considered the best among all gifts,
so is the Ekādaśī vow declared to be the best among all vows.

Just as there is no friend like religious merit, and no teacher like the sacred scripture,
even so there is no vow equal to Ekādaśī in the three worlds.

Just as the mind is declared by the wise to be the best of the sense-organs,
Kārtika is the best of months, and Arjuna is the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas;

just as the Vedas are proclaimed to be the best of all sacred texts,
so is the Ekādaśī vow remembered as the foremost among vows.

In the Vedas, the Āgamas, the Purāṇas, and other sacred texts, O twice-born,
no vow has ever been declared by the learned to be equal to Ekādaśī.

All human beings on the earthly realm may dwell without fear;
having observed the Ekādaśī vow, what can the son of the Sun (Yama) do?

What can Yama do to those who properly observe a single Ekādaśī?
Therefore, the Ekādaśī vow, which bestows auspiciousness, must indeed be performed.

I shall explain the procedure for the Ekādaśī vow in brief.
Becoming focused in mind, listen, O Jaimini, best of men!

Rising early on the tenth lunar day (Daśamī), one should clean one's teeth.
Then, avoiding oil, one should bathe, renouncing grain.

Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, with water for the feet and other offerings,
intent on meditation upon Hari, one should eat only a single meal.

Meat, salt, flesh, lentils,
large black gram, and leafy vegetables should be avoided on the tenth lunar day.

Eating twice, food given by others, honey, sexual intercourse,
and eating from bell-metal vessels should be avoided on the tenth lunar day.

Neem leaves, eggplant, burnt food, citron,
and cow's milk products devoid of ghee should be avoided on the tenth lunar day.

Eating excessively, eating too frequently,
and chewing betel leaves should be avoided on the tenth lunar day.

Whatever items are forbidden on the tenth lunar day, O best of the twice-born,
those very items are forbidden on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī) as well; of this there is no doubt.

On the tenth lunar day, O tiger among Brāhmaṇas, and also on the twelfth, a Vaiṣṇava
desiring the full fruit of the vow should not eat at night.

Therefore, having taken sacrificial food (haviṣya) on the tenth lunar day, the vow-keeper, being prompt,
should again clean his teeth according to rule in the afternoon.

In the evening, having gone to the temple of God and taken an offering of flowers,
meditating on Keśava in his mind, he should utter this mantra:

'This vow has been undertaken by me in your presence, O Govinda;
may it reach completion without obstacles by the compassion of your feet!

I am a man of extremely fickle mind, filled with greed and delusion;
how could I be able to observe this vow without your grace?'

Having recited these two verses, having offered that very handful of flowers
to Nārāyaṇa, he should then prostrate on the ground like a staff.

In that very temple of Viṣṇu, intent on the remembrance of Viṣṇu,
having spread a bed with kuśa grass on the bare ground, he should sleep.

Then, at dawn, when it is bright, he should not clean his teeth [with a stick];
rather, the wise person should cleanse his mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water.

He should perform the daily rites and the rites of worship to Viṣṇu and the like;
then, at night, O chief of Brāhmaṇas, along with all the people observing vows,

he should keep a vigil together before the Lord of the worlds,
accompanied by his mother, his wife, his brother, and his father,

and likewise accompanied by his sons and friends, he should keep a vigil for Hari.
Such an observer of the vow, O twice-born, shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu for a long time.

Whoever draws an image of the conch, discus, and the like in the temple of Viṣṇu,
Janārdana takes away the sins committed by him across many births.

If one draws an image in the sanctuaries of Viṣṇu with a paste of rice flour
or with other forest materials, hear the fruit of that:

Along with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, he enjoys all good fortune;
at the end, having gone to the city of Viṣṇu, he attains liberation there.

A person who hoists a flag on the day of the Lord of Kamalā,
having delivered ten million ancestors, goes to the city of Nārāyaṇa.

A person who adorns the temple of Viṣṇu adorned with rows of banners
shall obtain the status of an earthly king in birth after birth.

As long as the banner waves in the wind,
for that long every sin of its maker is destroyed.

Circles of banners of various colors should be erected in the house of Hari by the wise
who desire the supreme abode on the day of Hari.

A person who holds a very beautiful parasol over the head of Viṣṇu,
O seer among Brāhmaṇas, becomes a king (kṣattrī) on the earth in birth after birth.

A person who erects a floral pavilion on the day of Vāsudeva
obtains for each flower the merit of more than a hundred horse sacrifices.

Decorating with fragrant flowers on the day of Vāsudeva
should be performed diligently by the wise for the attainment of the fruit of the four aims of life.
One who builds a pavilion of cloth on Hari’s day / becomes an inhabitant of a palace in the dwelling of the gods, O brahmin sage.
Having constructed a cloth house, that person attaches there / white, red, or dark [cloth], beloved of Acyuta.
Having bathed the Śāligrāma stone or the image of the Lord of Śrī / with the five nectars, the vow-observer should install it there with devotion.
First the wise person should perform the invocation of blessing and the formal resolve; / it must be done with effort to attain the fruit of the four aims of life.
[He should perform] his own purification of the elements, O brahmin, according to the injunctions taught in the scriptures; / and then, single-minded, taking an excellent flower,
meditating on the god Nārāyaṇa residing in the lotus of the heart, / seated on a golden seat and also on one made of jewels:

‘Seated on a golden seat, adorned with sparkling ornaments of jewels, wearing a playful guise, bearing a delightful body radiant like a bright flashing cloud, / with four long arms, always shining, [holding weapons] in all his graceful hands, with lotus-eyes seeing the face of Śrī—I ceaselessly worship with a sidelong glance that [form] which removes all weariness.’
‘Come, O Lord, O God, united [with Lakṣmī], beloved Lord of Śrī! / Indeed, with devotion I must perform worship of you during this vow.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, together with Lakṣmī, O teacher of the world, / remain upon this excellent seat as long as I perform your worship.
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose fame is renowned throughout all the worlds! / Is all well with you? Tell me all, O you who are worshiped by the gods!’
‘Accept this fragrant water for the feet, O Lord of the gods, Nārāyaṇa, / which removes dust from the two feet, and is pure and very cool.
I give you water-offering, O Viṣṇu, joined with shoots of dūrvā grass / and accompanied by unbroken rice-grains, O lotus-eyed one.
I give you this very pure sipping water; / accept it, O supreme bliss, you who increase supreme bliss.
By the fragrant perfume given by me, O destroyer of Jarāsandha, / may your body be adorned, O Lord of Lakṣmī.
I give this sipping water for the sake of purity, / O cause of the beginning of the worlds, O God! Accept it, O Lord of the gods.
This incense was created by Brahmā long ago to increase the delight of the gods; / therefore this incense is given to you by me, O best of the gods.
Destroyer of the mass of darkness, filled with clarified butter, O Janārdana, / may this lamp be for your delight, O God, O Janārdana.
I give this garment with an upper cloth, very beautiful for the lower belly and the hips, / together with a sacred thread, O Lord of the gods, teacher of the world.
Food of four kinds, savory, accompanied by the six tastes, / has been offered by me with devotion; accept it, O Supreme Lord.
Remover of bad breath from the mouth, accompanied by camphor and catechu— / accept this betel, O Viṣṇu, giver of liberation, O highly wise one!’
According to this rite, surrounded by devotion, he should worship Govinda / with unsurpassed offerings during all four watches of the night.
Whoever would offer various presentations to Hari on Hari’s day— / crookedness regarding wealth should not be practiced by one desiring the fruit of actions.
Then indeed, a night-vigil should be kept by all the observers of the vow / devoted to Nārāyaṇa, with dance, song, hymns, and the like.
Circumambulation, O best of brahmins, and the names of the Lord of Kamalā, / destroying all sins, should be remembered by those engaged in the vow.
Those people who hear the sound of the name of Hari / resounding from every mouth shall be freed from great heaps of sin.
No conversation with heretics should be held on Hari’s day; / merely by talking with a heretic all religious merit is destroyed.
Hearing the song of Nārāyaṇa's fame poured out from each throat, / foolish people are not delighted, just as dogs [are not delighted by] the sound of a lute.
The virtuous experience joy upon hearing the song of the Lord of the world, / which destroys all sins, just as deer [delight in] the sound of a lute.
Singing the songs of Hari, they dance an excellent dance; / seeing this, the observers of the vow are delighted, [and the attendants] of the Lord of Kamalā are delighted.
The vow-observers who are not delighted in the temple of Viṣṇu, O brahmin— / perpetual bestiality would be theirs in birth after birth.
The observers of the vow who do not sing songs on Hari’s day / wander in birth after birth deprived of speech.
Musical instruments such as the mṛdaṅga drum should be played before Hari, / because the blessed Madhusūdana becomes pleased by instruments.
Keeping the night-vigil of Viṣṇu, the excellent recitation of the Veda / or the reading of the Purāṇas should be performed by Vaiṣṇava people.
The Rāmāyaṇa, the Bhāgavata, the Mahābhārata spoken by Vyāsa, / and other Purāṇas should be read on Hari’s day.
Those who read before Viṣṇu, and those who listen on Hari’s day, / obtain at every syllable the fruit born of gifting a brown cow.
A Vaiṣṇava person should joyful keep a vigil at night; / having thoroughly conquered sleep, he meditates upon Keśava in his heart.
In the manner of a circumambulation, again and again on Hari’s day, / falling like a staff upon the ground, he should bow down to Janārdana.
Then at clean dawn, having performed the five great sacrifices, / the devoted vow-observer, having bathed Hari with milk, should worship [him].
He should give a sacrificial fee for the vow to a brahmin according to his ability; / then within the twelfth day the vow-observer should break the fast.
He who breaks the fast having transgressed the twelfth lunar day, / the merit earned by him in ten million lifetimes is destroyed.
The breaking of the fast should be done by the wise within the twelfth lunar day, / never on the thirteenth by those desiring the fruit of the vow.
On the day of fasting, O brahmin, and also during the night, a Vaiṣṇava / who seeks to attain the fruit of fasting should carefully avoid sleep.
Without a night-vigil, fasting is truly useless; / therefore a night-vigil must be performed during both fortnights.
Those who perform the Ekādaśī vow according to this rite, / truly, truly, O best of brahmins, all of them go to liberation.

It is the sole cause of removing birth and death; it should be performed even by the hosts of gods led by Indra; / do you ceaselessly and diligently observe this essence of vows on the day of Vāsudeva, O Jaimini!

7.23.m: Vyāsa said: / Formerly, on the circle of the earth, there was a king named Kocarāśa, / peaceful, supremely knowledgable in dharma, the best of those who know royal policy,
truth-speaking, his anger conquered, all his enemies subdued, / dedicated to the worship of Nārāyaṇa, supreme in his devotion to Hari’s service.
His queen was named Suprajñā, sweet-speaking, / endowed with all auspicious marks, devoted to the service of her husband,
engaged in the Ekādaśī vow, wishing well for all living beings, / remembering her former births, highly fortunate, well-conducted, and fair-complexioned.
Having observed the tenth [lunar day], that king, who knew the supreme truth, / together with his wife, set out to keep a vigil in the night of the eleventh.
In the meantime, a certain brahmin named Śauri, endowed with great splendor, / came to the pavilion of the king's vigil.
As he arrived, that king, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / together with his wife, exceedingly delighted, honored him with water for the feet and the like.
Seated comfortably in their midst, that brahmin, who knew the reality of all things, / saw there many vow-observers dedicated to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Some worship Hari with various delightful flowers, / with fragrant scents, incenses, and lamps, and with unsurpassed offerings.
Some, adorned with clay from the Gaṅgā and decorated / with garlands of tulasī leaves, dance joyfully before Hari as observers of the vow.
Others sing delightful songs of Hari again, / taking up cymbals, observers of the vow, dear to the Blessed Lord.
With unsurpassed hymns, some praise the flawless Nārāyaṇa, / the Lord of the worlds, with divine meanings and gentle syllables.
With the cool breeze of white fly-whisks, for the Lord of the world, / some fan Hari with great affection.
Some great-souled ones play instruments such as the lute, / lovely, pure, and auspicious; others sing of Keśava.
Both the king and the chief queen, exceedingly joyful, / sang a charming song and danced an exquisite dance.
To that noble couple who were performing dancing, singing, and the like, / the eminent brahmin Śauri spoke with sweet words.
Śauri said: / Fortunate are you, O king, and fortunate is your queen! / This auspicious conduct of you two is hard to find in the world.
I shall tell you, since no one has seen such an eminent Vaiṣṇava: / by you as ruler of the earth, this earth is blessed; there is no doubt in this.
This holy Ekādaśī vow, dear to the Blessed Lord, / you perform together with your wife, O king; therefore you are foremost among Vaiṣṇavas.
You are the sole lord of the seven continents, together with your wife, O best of kings, / since with love you dance and sing before Nārāyaṇa.
