This conduct of you two, husband and wife, is seen to be wonderful. / From what has this exceedingly pure intellect of yours arisen?
Vyāsa said: / Having heard these words of the twice-born named Śauri, / Suprājñā, smiling slightly, then addressed that twice-born.
Suprājñā said: / By the power of Ekādaśī formerly, O best of the twice-born, / we two, great sinners, were released by the noble-souled son of the Sun.
Through the power of memory of our past births, O chief of brahmins, / we now observe the divine Ekādaśī vow, desiring the supreme abode.
Śauri said: / If indeed, O fair-hipped lady, you know your own / previous birth, tell it to me; curiosity has arisen in my heart to hear it.
Who were you formerly, and who was your husband? / How were you two, although sinners, released by the son of Bhāskara?
Suprājñā said: / Although these words are not to be disclosed, O best of the twice-born, / I was a chief courtesan, skilled in the treatise on erotic love.
In that birth, very many terrible sins / were committed by me, O chief of brahmins, which surely inflict the torments of hell.
This man was a Śūdra named Nityodaya, devoid of proper conduct, / an abductor of others' wives, cruel, a stealer of others' wealth,
a drinker of liquor, a killer of friends, a destroyer of embryos, injurer of others, / full of extreme pride, and always a reviler of dharma.
Once, completely abandoned by all his kinsmen of good vows, / longing for the charms of a courtesan, he came to my house.
Seeing him to be young and handsome, O best of the twice-born, / I too felt affection, and he was satisfied with sexual pleasures.
Then, having enjoyed sexual union with me, O ascetic, / he addressed me in love, bowing down with humility, with these words:
“I am an expert in the treatise on sexual love, abandoned by my own relatives. / If you approve, I shall remain there with you.”
Hearing this speech bowed down with humility, O twice-born, / I remained with him, assuming the state of husband and wife.
Once, O tiger among the twice-born, on the lunar day of Ekādaśī sacred to Hari, / I was tormented by great bodily afflictions that strike down the body.
On that very day, O best of the twice-born, with my body shattered by fever, / water was not drunk, nor was food eaten out of great fear.
And he, having an upsurge of affection for me, on that very day of Hari, / abandoned food and water, dejected on account of me, O twice-born.
Then at night, O best of the twice-born, having lit a lamp with ghee, / a vigil was kept by me, whose mind was stricken by fever.
Constantly babbling, “Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, protect me!” / a vigil at night was also kept by him.
By the power of fasting and the utterance of Keśava, / all the sin of both of us was destroyed, O twice-born.
Then, at pure daybreak, when the blessed Sun had risen, / afflicted by fever, I passed away, O best of brahmins.
Seeing that I had passed away, this man, pure [in affection], / then went to his death together with me, censured by all people.
Then, bound with a tight noose by the messengers of the Sun's son, / whose eyes were like blazing fire, we were led along an impassable path.
By the command of Yama, the wise Citragupta / investigated everything from the root, whether auspicious or inauspicious deed.
Citragupta said: / “Although these two, O mighty-armed one, are foremost among great sinners, / nevertheless, through fasting on Ekādaśī, they are freed from sins.
Even one who performs the holy Ekādaśī vow involuntarily / goes to the supreme abode, freed from all sins.”
Addressed thus by Citragupta, Dharmarāja of great renown / rose quickly from his seat and bowed to her and to him.
With fragrant, divine sandalpastes, incenses, and flowers, by Death / the two of them were adorned with golden ornaments, freed from sin.
With various sweet fruits like nectar, / the son of Bhāskara affectionately had a meal served to us two.
Then, having personally praised the two of us with divine hymns, the lord Yama / placed us on a divine chariot and spoke thus with joined palms:
Yama said: / "You two are the foremost of the virtuous, completely freed from all sin. / Go now to that place where the blessed Lord Viṣṇu resides."
When thus addressed by Dharmarāja, who was bowed down with humility, / this was then spoken by the two of us, having bowed to his lotus feet:
"O god, we must indeed go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, not otherwise; / yet the two of us have a desire to see hell, which is situated in your abode."
Then, by Yama's command, O brāhmaṇa, having mounted the splendid chariot, / the hells, difficult to behold, were seen by the two of us there in extensive detail.
The brāhmaṇa said: / "O devoted wife, you ought to recount in detail / all the conditions of the sinners that were seen there.
Tell me in detail, O fair-hipped one, / by which path the virtuous go to Yama's abode, and by which the sinful;
and of what form the virtuous behold the lord Vaivasvata there, / and the road of the virtuous and of the sinners, yielding pleasure and pain."
Suprājñā said: / "First I shall describe the path of virtuous men. / Listen, O tiger among the twice-born; it increases the joy of those who hear it.
Paved with wide stones and covered with divine garments, / the path of the virtuous shines, free from all afflictions.
In some places wondrous singing is sung by gandharva maidens; / in others dancing is performed by apsarases with charming bodies.
In some places they made the delightful strumming of the vīṇā and various instruments; / in some places there is a shower of flowers, and in some places a cool breeze.
In some places there are water booths with cool water, and in others dining halls; / in some places gods and gandharvas recite the highest hymn of praise.
Here and there are oblong ponds with blooming, beautiful lotuses, / and in some places are well-shaded trees, blossoming vañjulas and the like.
Then men endowed with happiness proceed along the path, / virtuous souls, O best of the twice-born, having attained an easy death.
Some, mounted on horses and adorned with various ornaments, / go covering their heads with white umbrellas held on tall poles.
Some go mounted on elephants, others mounted on chariots, / and some people, mounted on conveyances, happily reach Yama's abode.
Some mortals go fanned by breezes from flywhisks held in the hands of divine women, / being praised by celestial sages.
Some, bearing divine weapons and adorned with garlands and sandalwood, / go to Yama's abode chewing betel, being virtuous souls.
Some, illuminating the ten directions by the radiance of their own limbs, / dwellers of the heavenly spheres, go to the house of the Restrainer.
And some, O best of men, go eating divine milk-rice; / enjoying good food, they proceed happily on the road.
Some drinking milk, some likewise sugarcane juice, / and some drinking buttermilk go to Yama's abode.
Some eating curds, some various fruits, / and some drinking honey go, being virtuous souls.
Then, seeing many of those devoted to dharma arrived, / the son of the Sun, attaining joy, himself became Nārāyaṇa—
four-armed, dark-complexioned, with eyes like blooming lotuses, / holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, having Garuḍa as his mount,
wearing a golden sacred thread, with a noble face handsome as the god of love, / crowned, wearing earrings, and adorned with a forest garland.
The wise Citragupta and the servants of Yama such as Caṇḍa / all assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa, having sweet words.
Then Dharmarāja himself, attaining supreme joy, / would honor all those best among men like friends, O twice-born,
and, causing a meal of divine jewels and fruits to be served / to those virtuous men, the son of the Sun then spoke to them:
Yama said: / "You all are great souls, fearing the afflictions of hell; / by virtue of your own actions, go to the supreme abode!
The man who, having obtained birth in this worldly cycle, performs virtue / is my father, is my brother, is my kinsman, is my friend."
Addressed thus by Dharmarāja, all of them, O best of the twice-born, / mounted a celestial chariot and went to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
The destination of the virtuous has been declared in brief, O best of the twice-born. / Hear the destination of the sinful; I shall tell it in detail.
Eighty-six thousand yojanas / is said to be the length of the road for the wicked, and it is filled with all kinds of misery.
In some places there is a shower of fire, and in others a rain of stones; / here and there, O best of the twice-born, the scorched sand is heated.
Here and there are sharp stones, and likewise heated stones; / here and there a rain of weapons, and in some places a shower of live coals.
In some places winds blow, intensely burning like fire; / in some places are deep darknesses, O twice-born, bearing whirlwinds at their forefront.
In some places there is a shower of thorns made of iron spikes; / in some places are rows of rocks, difficult to climb, infested with serpents.
Sinners go there with dry throats, lips, and palates, / through such manifold misery, devoid of shade and water.
On that path, O best of the twice-born, sinners go suffering, / naked, with disheveled hair, terrible with the appearance of ghosts.
Some drenched in streams of blood, some smeared with mud, / and some with blackened limbs—the sinners go on the road.
Some crying out in pain, their eyes filled with flowing tears, / lamenting their own deeds, some sinners go along.
Of someone, the binding of a leather noose is on the sinner's neck; / some are bound by the skeleton, and someone by both feet.
Having placed a tight noose around the neck pierced with needles, / the messengers of Yama angrily drag some of them who have committed sins.
Carrying heavy stones lying on the path by their ear cavities, / and loads of iron on the tips of their heads, the sinners proceed on the road.
The servants of Yama lead some by nooses around their arms, / and some sinners by their necks with hard blows of the hand.
Constantly hurled, the servants of Yama lead Yama's messengers; / some go head downward, and others feet upward.
Some go on their arms, and others on one foot; / thus, misshapen in form, crying out with screams of distress,
beaten by Yama's messengers, the sinners proceed along that path. / When all those sinful souls arrived, Yama, in fury,
cast off his divine form and became exceedingly terrifying: / thirty yojanas long in body, with eyes like reservoirs,
smoke-colored, of great splendor, towering, with a rattling roar, / having an extremely long row of teeth, and claws resembling winnowing baskets,
mounted on a fierce buffalo, biting his lip, / with staff in hand, holding a leather noose, with a face crooked with a frown.
Citragupta of great power, his eyes reddened with anger, / laughing uproariously, and the Impartial One [Yama] shine forth.
All the servants, Caṇḍa and the rest, holding nooses and clubs in their hands, / became terrible, enraged, roaring like rainclouds.
"Kill, kill the wicked ones at once! Pierce, cut, break [them]!" / Running around on every side, Yama's servants pranced about.
To all those sinners falling before him, Lord Dharmarāja spoke, / threatening them with his rod of death and letting forth roaring shouts:
Yama said: / "O you sinners, evil-doers, thoughtless fools! / Alas, what sins you committed, causing torment even to yourselves!
Did you not see Samavartin standing over your head? / Though knowing me to be the lord of life, you committed sins!
'I am the kin of the virtuous; I am the enemy of the sinful.' / Was this never heard anywhere by your ears?
'The hells are unbearable, full of varied torments, / and sinners suffer them.' Was this not renowned among you?
Thinking of me as merely a myth, you evil-minded ones spoke lightly of me. / Today let it be seen with your own eyes, you who committed sins!
Blinded by wealth and intoxicated by your speech, all of you / constantly spun webs of sin, as you pleased.
So now, O wicked ones, reap the fruit of your sins! What use is weeping?" / Having spoken thus, the divine son of the sun, Suprājña, spoke to Citragupta:
"Examine the sinful deeds of these ones, O blessed one!" / Hearing Dharmarāja's words, the great Citragupta then,
prompted [by him], declared as many sins as they had committed. / Thereupon, O best of the twice-born, all those sinners wept.
Bound by leather straps, terrified, they said to Śamana: / The sinners said: / "Whatever sins were committed by us, O son of the sun,
who were the witnesses present there? Or who reported them to you? / For whatever evil or good was done by us in the past,
and whatever was seen by whom here, let that be declared before us!" / Then, laughing aloud in great anger, O twice-born,
the blessed one summoned all the witnesses and spoke these words: / Yama said: / "You all [speak] in this presence just as it occurred, as witnesses!"
The sky, the earth, water, and the lunar days, / day, night, both twilights, and Dharma—these were the witnesses.
They proclaimed every deed, good and bad, of those sinful souls: / at whatever time whichever action was caused to be done,
the corresponding witness declared it in the presence of Yama. / Hearing that, all the sinners, their minds seized with dread,
stood with trembling hearts, like deer that have seen a cloud. / Then, making a cracking sound with his rows of teeth,
Dharmarāja struck them one by one with the rod of death. / Beaten by Dharmarāja, all those perpetrators of sin
wept, grieving over their deeds, seized with terror. / Then the messengers, Caṇḍa and the others, in fury
cast all those sinners into hells such as Raurava by Yama's order. / They threw some into Tapana, and sinners into Avīci;
into Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, and Mahārauravaka, / and into the boiling bed of sand, and others into Kumbhīpāka;
into Nirucchvāsa, Mahāghora, and they threw them into Pramardana, / into the dreadful Asipatravana, and into the [hells of] various foods, the sinners;
and Yama's servants cast some into Vaitaraṇī. / In the dreadful lake of feces, and some into [a hell] with husks, burning coals, bones, and thorns,
filled [with horrors] and extremely scorching, Yama's servants threw them. / In smearing with feces and eating feces,
and in eating their own flesh they were placed by Yama's servants. / Some eat phlegm, and some eat semen;
some sinners drink urine, and some drink blood. / Right into the mouths of some, leeches resembling serpents
and serpents are stuffed by Yama's dreadful messengers; / and their tongues are pulled out with scorching-hot [tongs], O best of the twice-born.
Into the ear-holes and mouths of some perpetrators of sin, / boiling oils are poured by the merciless servants of Yama.
With sword blades they cut off the arms and feet / and the ears and noses of some wicked ones.
Some lie upon heaps of blazing coals; / some lie upon thorns sharp as iron arrows.
And into boiling mud the servants of Śamana / throw some sinners, dragging them by their hair, O best of the twice-born.
Into the vomits and nail-joints of some sinners, / they repeatedly plunge thousands of heated needles.
They impale some on the point of a red-hot iron stake; / they weep as the heads of some are [pierced] with sharp thorns.
Seizing them by the hands and feet, with the thorns of the silk-cotton tree / they violently scrape some who scream with cries of agony.
Binding stones to the necks of some, Śamana's servants / repeatedly cast them into pits of blood and pits of water.
By Yama's messengers the heads of sinful men are made to vomit [blood]; / with stones, Yama's servants crush them repeatedly in extreme rage.
Into the chests of some of the weeping, wicked souls, / they drive clusters of iron spikes.
The eyes of some perpetrators of sin are torn out with fishhooks; / the nostrils of some are filled with scorpions, O twice-born.
Binding the feet of some to tree branches with nooses, / Yama's servants kindle a smoky fire beneath [them].
There those wrongdoers inhale smoke; / hanging head downward with feet upward, they remain as long as the moon and stars endure.
Struck again and again by Yama's messengers with pestles and clubs, / some vomit blood, overwhelmed by agony.
In a house full of darkness and foul odor, O twice-born, / some sinners waste away, plagued by stinging flies and mosquitoes.
Some eat ashes, and some eat worms; / some eat foul-smelling flesh, and some foul earth.
Being eaten by dogs, tigers, jackals with adamantine teeth and claws, / and bears, some weep, soaked in blood.
Others are devoured by serpents of exceedingly fierce poison; / others, their chests split open by the tips of buffalo horns, O twice-born,
fall unconscious, drenching the earth far and wide with their blood. / By dreadful [arrows] loosed from the bows of Yama's messengers, like venomous serpents,
others roll on the ground, their whole bodies shattered. / An abode of red-hot iron lumps and heated stones [they endure];
with stinging weapons they tear into the mouths of some; / and into the nostrils and mouths of some, Yama's messengers
weave [shut] their nostrils to stop the breath of air; / and with sharp-edged, terrible spears of Yama,
the skin of the limbs of some is ripped off by Yama's mighty messengers. / Seizing some by the hair and hurling them to the earth,
they constantly beat them with stakes, kicks, and blows. / Tormented by streams of alkaline water, some who committed sins
drink alkaline water, wailing loudly, O twice-born; / some sinners drink bile, O blessed one.

And some eminent sinners drink the milk of the spurge tree.
Upon the chests of some who lie on the ground, the servants of Yama

place heavy stones, heated and like mountains.
Placing two pieces of wood upon the neck and at the throat,

they bind their faces pointing upward with tight nooses.
Lifting some onto tree branches, they cast them to the ground;

they raise them up and throw them down on the ground again and again.
Thus all those sinners, hungry and thirsty,

wail in the house of torment, crying out: "Save us! Save us!"
Having experienced the torments of hell until the end of yugas and kalpas,

having suffered intensely, with the residue of their sin they are born in sinful wombs.
Born in a sinful womb, they are afflicted with diseases,

with deficient limbs or extra limbs, miserable, devoted to sin,
sonless, utterly foolish, and intent on harming others,

short-lived, dull-witted, and husbands of bad wives.
Always [committing] sinful actions with deed, mind, and speech,

they go to hell again, as before, through the power of sin.
Therefore sin should never be committed by good men;

for men who have committed sins, there is no release from hell.
In brief, the suffering of sinners has been explained, O best of the twice-born.

Who is able to describe it fully even in hundreds of myriads of years?
Then, having seen the miserable plight of men who committed sins,

we two mounted an aerial chariot and went to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
Having enjoyed pleasures in the abode of Hari for thousands of crores of kalpas,

we were born into this pure Vairāja lineage, O best of the twice-born.
Here, having enjoyed all pleasures accompanied by all prosperity,

and attaining a comfortable death, we must go to the supreme state.
In the three worlds there is no vow equal to the Ekādaśī vow,

by performing which even unintentionally such was the destiny of us two.
Those who undertake the Ekādaśī vow with a devotional disposition,

I do not know what might become of them through the compassion of Vāsudeva!
Thus all that you asked has been told to you, O best of Brahmins,

the glorification of the day of Viṣṇu. What else do you wish to hear?
Vyāsa said: Having heard his words, that Brahmin who knew the highest truth

fixed his mind very firmly upon the Ekādaśī vow.
That king and the chief queen, having long enjoyed the earth,

went in the end to the city of Viṣṇu and attained the supreme state.
Those who hear or recite this glorification of the king of vows,
freed from the snares of sin, obtain [a place] in the presence of Hari.
